newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong democrats plan protest at handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong democrats plan protest at handover.

text.p: Leaders of Hong Kong's democracy movement threw down a gauntlet to Chinese authorities on Tuesday by vowing to force their way into parliament as the world watches Britain hand the territory back to China.

Across the border, in an unrelated development, China put its army on alert and pushed for its troops to be allowed to march into Hong Kong before Beijing officially regains control of the territory on July 1.
The actions were signs of fraying nerves on both sides as what China has described as the media event of the century approaches.

At midnight on June 30 the British Union Jack will be lowered, Prince Charles will hand Hong Kong back to China's President Jiang Zemin, and the red flag of Communist China will be hoisted, marking an end to 156 years of colonial rule.

The potentially biggest flashpoint was a plan announced by Hong Kong's beleaguered Democratic Party, Hong Kong's biggest political group, to challenge official bans on protests during the handover ceremonies.
The Democratic Party acted after authorities blocked plans for public protest rallies by the Alliance in Support of the Patriotic Democratic Movement in China.
It would have been the first pro-democracy rally under Chinese rule.
The party plans a bold counter-move in the small hours of July 1 to clash with the new assembly's inauguration, party vice chairman Yeung Sum said.

Yeung said activists would make speeches of protest in the doomed Legislative Council chamber, which is near the Convention Centre where the heavily-guarded handover ceremony and gala will take place.
An aide told reporters: "We will consider a non-peaceful operation, if authorities block our way in."
Beijing plans to swear-in its own hand-picked legislature at the Convention Centre shortly after midnight, formally replacing Hong Kong's democratically-elected parliament.
Representatives of the Democratic Party will attend the handover ceremony but try to steal the limelight when members of the provisional legislative council take their oaths.
It was China's worst fear for the gala handover night which is to be attended by 4,000 VIP guests and beamed around the world via satellite.
Some 8,000 journalists from around the world will be closely watching China's response to any signs of unrest after it resumes power.
Britain and the United States have threatened to boycott the swearing-in ceremony to protest against China's plans to scrap the territory's existing legislature.
Earlier in the day Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, appointed by China, sparked fresh suspicions by announcing changes to the lower tiers of government in a further rollback for democracy.
Tung, who takes over on July 1, unveiled measures to dilute the presence of pro-democracy politicians in local government by appointing extra pro-China figures to local councils.
China meanwhile has put its three-million-strong People's Liberation Army and police force on high alert against unrest in the run-up to the Hong Kong handover.

The People's Liberation Army, the paramilitary People's Armed Police, police and security agents have gone on high alert in Beijing and in other parts of China in case of ethnic unrest or internal instability, reports from Beijing said.
"The authorities are worried the jobless and the democracy movement will create trouble," one source there said.
British officials were tight-lipped about China's late request for its troops to arrive in Hong Kong ahead of time.

Beijing already has an advance party of about 200 People's Liberation Army (PLA) soldiers in Hong Kong but wants to send more over the border before midnight on June 30 to allow the troops to be in place the minute Chinese rule begins.
On Monday, China's top official on the JLG said Beijing thought it necessary to deploy more troops before the handover.
"There is a practical need. It is a matter that needs to be resolved and we hope to solve it," Zhao Jihua said.
